Signs your windows are ready to be replaced You do not have to wait for a pane to shatter. These are the signals we see most in Cache Valley homes: Fog or moisture between the panes. That is a failed seal on a double-pane unit. The insulating gas is gone and the window is not doing its job anymore. Sometimes the fix is glass-only; sometimes the unit is old enough that replacement makes more sense. Drafts you can feel. Hold a hand near the frame edges on a windy day. If you feel moving air with the window locked, you are paying to heat the outdoors. Windows that stick, drop, or will not lock. A window you cannot open is a safety problem in a bedroom, and a window that will not lock is a security problem everywhere. Condensation and ice on the inside every winter morning. Some interior condensation is humidity, but heavy, recurring ice-up usually means the window itself is underperforming. Rooms that never hold temperature. If one room runs cold every winter and hot every July, its windows are the first suspects. Rot, soft spots, or peeling around the frame. Once water is in the wood, patching is temporary. Replacement stops the damage from spreading into the wall. One or two of these on a newer window might just mean a repair. Several of them on windows past their twentieth birthday usually means it is time. Either way, the estimate is free and we will give you the honest read. What you are actually choosing when you pick new windows The window itself matters as much as the install. A few plain-English basics we will walk through with you: Double-pane glass is the standard now: two panes with an insulating space between them. If you are replacing single-pane windows from an older Logan or Hyrum home, this alone is the biggest comfort jump. Low-E coatings are microscopically thin metallic layers that reflect heat back where it came from: into the house in January, away from it in July. In a climate that swings from below zero to the high 90s like ours, low-E earns its keep in both directions. Frame material drives feel and maintenance. Vinyl is the value workhorse; fiberglass and clad-wood cost more and look and last like it. Style (single-hung, slider, casement, picture) is partly taste and partly function; egress rules also set minimums for bedroom windows, which we will flag where they apply. We carry quality lines including Marvin and Cascade Windows and will match the package to your house and budget at the estimate rather than upselling you a tier you do not need. How to tell what your screen actually needs You can usually diagnose a screen yourself in about ten seconds, which helps us give you a faster answer on the phone: Small hole or tear, frame straight and square? That is a rescreen. The frame stays, the mesh gets replaced. Cheapest fix there is. Mesh sagging or bellied out but not torn? The spline (the rubber cord that pins the mesh into the frame) has loosened or the mesh has stretched. A rescreen tightens it right back up. Corner popped apart or frame bent? Screen frames are held together with little plastic corner keys that get brittle in the sun. A single bad corner is often a quick repair; a frame that is bent along its length is usually better replaced. Screen falls out of the window or will not stay in the track? The frame has lost its shape or the spring pins are shot. We will check whether it is fixable or whether a new screen sized to the opening is the smarter buy. Screen missing entirely? No problem, and very common on homes that changed hands. We measure the opening and build a new one to fit. If you are not sure, that is fine too. Why screens matter more here than you think Cache Valley summers are made for open windows. The nights cool off hard, and running the house on night air instead of the AC is one of the quiet perks of living here, but only if your screens actually keep the bugs out. Come spring, the valley's canyon breezes and irrigation ditches bring out the mosquitoes and gnats, and a single torn screen is an open door for all of them. Our seasons are also why screens wear out. Winter means screens sit through months of freeze, snow load, and UV; some folks store them, most do not. Spring and summer wind off the Wellsville and Bear River ranges works the mesh loose and bends light frames. Kids, dogs, and the garden hose finish the job. By the time you want the windows open, half the screens in the house have a problem. We see the same wave every year from Logan and North Logan out through Smithfield, Providence, Hyrum, Nibley, Millville, and Hyde Park, and west into Tremonton and the Box Elder towns. The nice part: screens are cheap to fix relative to almost everything else in a house. A round of rescreening across a home costs a fraction of one window and buys back every open-window night of the summer. Choosing the right mesh Most people never think about screen mesh until they have a specific problem, and then it matters a lot. The main options: Standard fiberglass is the default: affordable, flexible, and fine for most windows, and it typically lasts around ten to twelve years before the mesh gets brittle. If your screens are just old and torn, this is almost certainly what goes back in. Fine no-see-um mesh has a tighter weave that stops the tiny biting gnats and sand flies that standard mesh lets through, which is worth it near water, fields, and irrigation. It also sharpens the view out. Pet-resistant mesh is a heavier vinyl-coated polyester weave, several times stronger than standard fiberglass, built to survive dogs and cats leaning, pawing, and pushing on it. If you have replaced the same screen twice because of a pet, this is the fix. Solar and shade screens use a denser mesh that blocks a large share of the sun's heat, glare, and UV before it ever hits the glass. On west- and south-facing windows that bake all afternoon, they cut cooling load and glare noticeably while you can still see out. We will suggest the mesh that fits your actual situation rather than defaulting everyone to the same roll. If you want the cheap standard mesh, that is a perfectly good answer too. Glass problems we fix Broken and cracked panes. Rocks from the lawnmower, hail, a slammed door, a kid's line drive. Whatever did it, we measure the opening, cut or order the right glass, and set it properly. If the break left your home open to the weather, ask about emergency board-up when you call; we can secure the opening the same day so you are not living with a hole in the house while the glass is on its way. Foggy double-pane windows. When moisture appears between the two panes of glass and will not wipe off from either side, the insulated unit's seal has failed. The window has lost the gas fill that made it efficient, and no amount of cleaning brings it back. The good news: in most cases we can replace just the sealed glass unit inside your existing frame. You keep the window, lose the fog, and pay a fraction of full replacement. Glass in doors. Sliding patio doors, French doors, front-door lites, and storm doors. Door glass is almost always tempered safety glass, which is a different animal from window glass, and we handle it routinely. A dragging slider with good glass is a hardware problem; a cracked panel in a good door is exactly what this page is about. Tempered and safety glass. Building code requires tempered safety glass in specific spots: in doors, in glass within two feet of a door, in low windows within 18 inches of the floor, and in and around tubs and showers. Tempered glass is heat-treated so that if it ever breaks it crumbles into small dull pebbles instead of blades, and it cannot be cut after it is made, so it has to be ordered to exact size. We know where code requires it, and we will not quietly put standard glass where safety glass belongs. Tabletops, shelves, and specialty pieces. Glass for furniture, cabinet doors, and replacement panes for older single-pane windows in Logan's historic homes. If it is flat glass for your home or business, ask; the answer is usually yes. (Custom shower glass and storefront glass each have their own page.) If the glass just broke, do this first Before anything else, deal with the sharp stuff and the opening: Keep kids and pets out of the room until the loose glass is up. Broken tempered glass crumbles into pebbles; broken standard glass leaves blades. Treat both with respect. Do not pull shards out of the frame. Panes under tension can release more glass when you tug on a piece. Leave what is stuck and let us pull it safely with the right gloves and tools. Sweep, then vacuum, wearing shoes. Glass travels farther than you think; check a ten-foot radius, and run a flashlight low across the floor to catch slivers the overhead light misses. Cover the opening. A layer of cardboard or plastic sheeting taped over the hole keeps weather and bugs out overnight. If the opening is big, ground-level, or you will be away, call us about same-day board-up instead; plywood beats plastic when security is part of the problem. Take photos before you clean up if there is any chance of an insurance claim. Adjusters like seeing the scene, not just the aftermath. Then call (435) 258-5456 and we will get the real fix moving.
